name: Weighted-average cost of capital (WACC)
expression: WACC = w_d r_d(1 − t) + w_p r_p + w_e r_e
meaning: Weighted required return across debt, preferred stock when present, and common equity.

variables.t: marginal tax rate when interest is deductible

intuition: Each source contributes its required return in proportion to the capital it supplies; only deductible interest receives the tax adjustment.
commonMistake: Using book and market weights inconsistently or applying the tax adjustment to equity.
relatedLearningOutcome: calculate and interpret the weighted-average cost of capital for a company

name: After-tax cost of debt
expression: After-tax cost of debt = r_d(1 − t)
meaning: Debt investors’ required return adjusted for tax-deductible interest.
intuition: Deductible interest shields taxable income, reducing the issuer’s effective debt cost.
workedExample: A 6% pretax debt cost at a 25% tax rate becomes 6%(1−0.25)=4.5%.
commonMistake: Applying the adjustment where interest is not deductible or treating it as a bond-pricing formula.
relatedLearningOutcome: calculate and interpret the weighted-average cost of capital for a company

name: Operating leverage
expression: Operating leverage = Fixed costs / Total costs
meaning: The proportion of total costs that is fixed under the official 2027 LM6 definition.

variables.Fixed costs: costs unchanged over the relevant activity range

intuition: A larger fixed-cost share makes operating profit more sensitive to changes in revenue.
workedExample: Fixed costs of 30 and total costs of 75 produce operating leverage of 40%.
commonMistake: Substituting degree of operating leverage or the FSA assets-to-equity financial-leverage ratio.
relatedLearningOutcome: explain factors affecting capital structure and the weighted-average cost of capital

name: MM Proposition I without taxes
meaning: Under restrictive frictionless assumptions, leverage does not change firm value.
intuition: Investors can create homemade leverage, so financing alone cannot change the value of unchanged operating cash flows.
workedExample: If the unlevered firm is worth 80, the otherwise identical levered firm is also worth 80.
commonMistake: Applying irrelevance after introducing tax shields or financial-distress costs.
relatedLearningOutcome: explain the Modigliani–Miller propositions regarding capital structure

name: MM Proposition II without taxes
meaning: Levered equity cost increases linearly with debt-to-equity when taxes are absent.
intuition: The increasing equity cost exactly offsets the use of cheaper debt, keeping WACC and value unchanged.
workedExample: r0=10%, rd=5%, and D/E=0.6 gives re=13%.
commonMistake: Adding the (1−t) adjustment in the no-tax case.
relatedLearningOutcome: explain the Modigliani–Miller propositions regarding capital structure

name: MM Proposition I with corporate taxes
meaning: Levered value equals unlevered value plus the present value of the debt tax shield under source assumptions.
intuition: Deductible interest adds value when offsetting distress costs are excluded.
commonMistake: Using the relationship when debt has no tax benefit or treating it as the full real-world optimum.
relatedLearningOutcome: explain the Modigliani–Miller propositions regarding capital structure

name: MM Proposition II with corporate taxes
meaning: Equity cost rises with leverage more slowly than in the no-tax case.
intuition: The tax shield lowers WACC and raises firm value as debt increases when distress costs are absent.
commonMistake: Concluding that 100% debt is realistic after ignoring distress and agency costs.
relatedLearningOutcome: explain the Modigliani–Miller propositions regarding capital structure
